questions.question: Why did the authors fit a lunar shadow velocity in addition to source size when modeling occultation fringes?

options.A: The uncertain lunar-limb shape can shift predicted shadow speed by tens of percent
options.B: The stellar pulsation changed the lunar angular diameter
options.C: The NaCl prism caused a time-dependent wavelength drift
options.D: The star's proper motion was comparable to the detector readout interval

questions.rationale: Limb irregularities make the predicted fringe speed uncertain.
questions.evidence_quote: uncertainties in the shape of the lunar limb

questions.question: Which limitation most directly prevented reliable detection of 10–30% departures from a uniform-disk photosphere in the comparison stars?

options.A: The Moon's phase was too close to new
options.B: Data/modeling accuracy was only about ±2 mas
options.D: The detector integrated for several seconds per frame

questions.rationale: Their angular-size accuracy was inadequate for sub-milliarcsecond departures.
questions.evidence_quote: accuracies on the order of ±2 mas.

questions.question: At what cadence was the detector read during AFGL 5440's lunar occultation, and what consequence did this have for the fringes?

options.A: Every 8 ms, so the Fresnel fringe pattern was time-averaged over each 8-ms integration
options.B: Every 80 ms, leaving the fringes effectively instantaneous
options.C: Every 8 s, requiring interpolation across many missing cycles
options.D: Every 1 ms, so no temporal averaging occurred

questions.rationale: The detector integrated essentially the full 8-ms frame, averaging the fringe pattern over that interval (and the telescope aperture).
questions.evidence_quote:
The detector is read-out every 8
msec, with photon integration occuring over essentially the full 8 msec time. Therefore, the
Fresnel occultation fringe pattern is averaged over this 8 msec time (as well as over the 2.7-m
telescope aperture).

questions.question: What observation argued against representing AFGL 5440 with one uniform-disk size over the full band?

options.A: An 11-mas disk gave fringes too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths
options.B: A disk fit only 1–2 μm and failed entirely above 2 μm
options.C: The fringe amplitude increased monotonically with wavelength
options.D: The 11-mas disk fit comparison stars but not AFGL 5440

questions.rationale: The test disk was passable only in the mid-band and mismatched opposite wavelength ends.
questions.evidence_quote:
To demonstrate
the poor ﬁt with a single size uniform disk, we show in Figures 5 and 6 the results of trying
to ﬁt the data with one example uniform disk, 11 mas. As can be seen in the plots of χ2
as well as the observed versus model light curves, the 11 mas disk provides a passable ﬁt in
the mid-range of wavelengths, 2.5 – 3.2µm, but produces fringes that are too sharp at the
longer wavelengths and too broadened at the shortest wavelengths.

questions.question: Which inner-shell temperature constraint emerged from combined occultation and SED modeling, and what set its lower bound?

options.A: 950 ± 50 K; below 900 K there was too little hot dust to blur long-wavelength fringes
options.B: 750 ± 50 K; cooler dust overproduced the 60-μm flux
options.C: 1200 ± 100 K; hotter dust could not reproduce the 11-μm SiC feature
options.D: 500 ± 50 K; colder dust was incompatible with stellar diameter

questions.rationale: Models below 900 K lacked enough warm dust for the observed near-IR occultation fringes.
questions.evidence_quote:
First, the dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell was of order 950K
± 50K. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot
dust to ﬁt the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths, while models with hotter inner
edges had even more diﬃculty than the best-ﬁt model in reproducing the energy distribu-
tion longward of 10µm.

questions.question: How did acceptable radial density laws behave across the near/mid-IR and far-IR constraints?

options.A: An r⁻²-like law fit occultation and SED broadly, but comparable graphite-free models failed at 60 μm
options.B: An r⁻¹ law fit occultation, while r⁻² fit only 60 μm
options.C: An r⁻²·² law uniquely fit fringes and solved the far-IR excess
options.D: A constant-density shell fit 3–60 μm but failed below 4 μm

questions.rationale: Favored profiles were close to r⁻²; the 60-μm mismatch remained absent graphite or altered outer-shell history.
questions.evidence_quote:
Secondly, the radial density gradient of models with a reasonable
ﬁt was close to r−2 (or to DUSTY’s calculation of the gradient appropriate for a radiatively
driven wind which approximates an r−2 distribution for large radii). Models with a density
gradient of r−1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm ﬂux, but did not ﬁt the shape of
the 5 – 20µm energy distribution well. Models with a density gradient of r−2.2 can ﬁt the
energy distribution out to 20µm and also provide a good ﬁt to the occultation results, but
have substantially worse ﬁts to the IRAS 60µm ﬂux than our best ﬁt models.

questions.question: What tradeoff resulted from changing the density gradient from r⁻² to r⁻¹·⁸?

options.A: It moved toward the IRAS 60-μm flux but worsened the 5–20-μm SED shape
options.B: It improved occultation fit but erased the 11-μm SiC feature
options.C: It fixed the 5–20-μm SED while substantially worsening 60 μm
options.D: It forced inner temperature below 900 K and optical depth to zero

questions.rationale: The shallower law increased longer-wavelength emission at the cost of the mid-IR fit.
questions.evidence_quote:
Models with a density
gradient of r−1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm ﬂux, but did not ﬁt the shape of
the 5 – 20µm energy distribution well.

questions.question: Why did the best-fitting SED model include substantial graphite despite contrary evidence from comparable carbon stars?

options.A: Its relatively flat 10–50 μm emissivity helped match the IRAS 60-μm flux
options.B: It alone created the 11-μm SiC feature
options.C: It lowered dust temperature to 750 K
options.D: It prevented 3–4 μm emission from blurring occultation fringes

questions.rationale: Amorphous carbon plus SiC alone underpredicted 60 μm by at least a factor of three.
questions.evidence_quote:
relatively ﬂat
emissivity vs. wavelength dependence between 10 and 50µm

questions.question: What alternative explanation did the authors offer for excess 60-μm emission if graphite is rejected?

options.A: Higher mass loss several hundred to a few thousand years ago left more cool dust at large radii
options.B: A recent increase placed extra hot dust inside the sublimation radius
options.C: A shorter distance shifted 11-μm emission into the 60-μm band
options.D: A faster present wind enlarged the inner shell in occultation

questions.rationale: 60-μm-emitting material lies far out and traces mass loss hundreds to thousands of years earlier.
questions.evidence_quote:
If the mass-loss rate
were greater in the past

questions.question: Which pair best represents reported recent mass-loss estimates and their comparison?

options.A: Dust 6.5×10⁻⁸ M☉/yr here versus 5.1×10⁻⁸ previously; gas about 3.1×10⁻⁵ M☉/yr
options.C: Dust 5×10⁻⁶ versus gas 6.5×10⁻⁸ M☉/yr, both from occultation
options.D: Dust 10⁻⁹ versus gas 10⁻⁶ M☉/yr with exact agreement

questions.rationale: The modeled dust rate slightly exceeded the prior estimate, while gas loss was hundreds-fold larger.
questions.evidence_quote:
The dust mass-loss rate implied by our derived optical depth
and radial density dependence is
˙M dust = 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr for the optical constants of
amorphous carbon used by DUSTY (Ivezi´c, Nenkova & Elitzur 1999). Groenewegen et al.
(2002) computed dust and gas mass-loss rates individually for AFGL 5440 on the basis of the
IRAS 60µm ﬂux for the dust, and millimeter CO observations for the gas. They derived a
gas mass-loss rate of 3.1×10−5 M⊙/yr and dust mass-loss rate of 5.1×10−8 M⊙/yr implying
a gas-to-dust mass ratio of 600. Interestingly, their dust mass-loss rate is slightly lower than
the value we have derived in spite of their using the 60µm IRAS ﬂux for normalization.
